By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.

articles.title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.17053v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) models typically represent clinical concepts as dataset-specific tokens, discarding their associated natural-language semantics. Consequently, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence without directly exploiting pretrained linguistic knowledge. We investigate the contribution of pretrained language semantics to longitudinal EHR prediction through tEHR, a framework that converts clinical events into natural-language descriptions and adapts pretrained autoregressive language models through EHR-specific continued pretraining and task-specific discriminative fine-tuning. We evaluate tEHR across four MIMIC-IV prediction tasks, where Mistral-7B achieves the strongest overall performance against structured-data, code-based, and LLM-based baselines. Controlled ablations demonstrate the importance of lexical grounding, numerical values, and both adaptation stages. A capacity-controlled experiment further shows that replacing clinical descriptions with atomic code tokens substantially reduces performance despite retaining the same LLM backbone. Alternative approaches incorporating pretrained semantic embeddings offer lower computational costs but do not match full textualisation. These results highlight the importance of both semantic representation and downstream adaptation when applying pretrained language models to structured EHR prediction.

articles.title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.18279v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.

articles.title: ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness
articles.summary:
arXiv:2503.08823v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for HDL generation, but existing benchmarks for LLM-based code generation primarily focus on functional correctness while overlooking hardware resource usage. Furthermore, current benchmarks offer limited diversity and do not fully represent the wide range of real-world FPGA applications. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ResBench, the first resource-focused benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish between resource-optimized and inefficient LLM-generated HDL code. ResBench consists of 56 problems across 12 categories, covering applications from finite state machines to financial computing. Our open-source evaluation framework automatically tests LLMs by generating Verilog code, verifying correctness, and measuring resource usage. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.

articles.title: BitBypass: A New Direction in Jailbreaking Aligned Large Language Models with Bitstream Camouflage
articles.summary:
arXiv:2506.02479v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The inherent risk of generating harmful and unsafe content by Large Language Models (LLMs), has highlighted the need for their safety alignment. Various techniques like supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and red-teaming were developed for ensuring the safety alignment of LLMs. However, the robustness of these aligned LLMs is always challenged by adversarial attacks that exploit unexplored and underlying vulnerabilities of the safety alignment. In this paper, we develop a novel black-box jailbreak attack, called BitBypass, that leverages hyphen-separated bitstream camouflage for jailbreaking aligned LLMs. This represents a new direction in jailbreaking by exploiting fundamental information representation of data as continuous bits, rather than leveraging prompt engineering or adversarial manipulations. Our evaluation of five state-of-the-art LLMs, namely GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3.5, Llama 3.1, and Mixtral, in adversarial perspective, revealed the capabilities of BitBypass in bypassing their safety alignment and tricking them into generating harmful and unsafe content. Further, we observed that BitBypass outperforms several state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks in terms of stealthiness and attack success. Overall, these results highlights the effectiveness and efficiency of BitBypass in jailbreaking these state-of-the-art LLMs.

articles.title: Revela: Dense Retriever Learning via Language Modeling
articles.summary:
arXiv:2506.16552v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Dense retrievers play a vital role in accessing external and specialized knowledge to augment language models (LMs). Training dense retrievers typically requires annotated query-document pairs, which are costly to create and scarce in specialized domains (e.g., code) or in complex settings (e.g., requiring reasoning). These practical challenges have sparked growing interest in self-supervised retriever learning. Since LMs are trained to capture token-level dependencies through a self-supervised learning objective (i.e., next token prediction), we can analogously cast retrieval as learning dependencies among chunks of tokens. This analogy naturally leads to the question: How can we adapt self-supervised learning objectives in the spirit of language modeling to train retrievers?
  To answer this question, we introduce Revela, a unified and scalable training framework for self-supervised retriever learning via language modeling. Revela models semantic dependencies among documents by conditioning next token prediction on local and cross-document context through an in-batch attention mechanism. This attention is weighted by retriever-computed similarity scores, enabling the retriever to be optimized as part of language modeling. We evaluate Revela on domain-specific (CoIR), reasoning-intensive (BRIGHT), and general-domain (BEIR) benchmarks across various retriever backbones. Without annotated or synthetic query-document pairs, Revela surpasses larger supervised models and proprietary APIs on both CoIR and BRIGHT. It achieves BEIR's unsupervised SoTA with ~1000x less training data and 10x less compute. Performance increases with batch size and model size, highlighting Revela's scalability and its promise for self-supervised retriever learning.

articles.title: SmartThinker: Learning High-Density Reasoning via Step-Level Token Allocation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2507.04348v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have exhibited remarkable reasoning capabilities through inference-time scaling, but this progress has also introduced considerable redundancy and inefficiency into their reasoning processes, resulting in substantial computational waste. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this issue by penalizing the overall length of generated samples during reinforcement learning (RL), with the goal of encouraging a more concise chains of Efficient reasoning is critical for large reasoning models (LRMs) deployed in agent systems with strict context constraints. Existing methods predominantly rely on global length penalties that overlook step-level structure, inadvertently compressing critical derivations while retaining low-value detours. Hence, we argue for a principled, step-aware alternative that preserves critical steps and compresses low-value detours. However, it raises three fundamental challenges: the difficulty of obtaining step-level supervision, the need for reward signals that induce differentiated length pressure, and the requirement to balance training stability with exploration on complex problems. We propose SmartThinker, a step-level token allocation framework that learns to selectively preserve or compress individual reasoning steps. At its core is Step-Level Length Control Policy Optimization (SCPO), which provides label-free feedback by online estimation of each step's contribution from the change in correct-answer likelihood after removing it. We further introduce reasoning density, defined as contribution per token, to relax length pressure on high-value steps while intensifying it on low-density ones. Finally, SCPO stabilizes training through length-bias-corrected advantages and difficulty-adaptive clipping, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across nine in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks.

articles.title: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.12915v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As the world becomes increasingly saturated with AI-generated content, disinformation, and algorithmic persuasion, critical thinking - the capacity to evaluate evidence, detect unreliable claims, and exercise independent judgment - is becoming a defining human skill. Developing critical thinking skills through timely assessment and feedback is crucial; however, there has not been extensive work in educational data mining on defining, measuring, and supporting critical thinking. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of measuring "subskills" that underlie critical thinking. We ground our work in an authentic task where students operationalize critical thinking by writing argumentative essays. We developed a coding rubric based on an established skills progression and completed human coding for a corpus of student essays. We then evaluated three distinct approaches to automated scoring: zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and supervised fine-tuning, implemented across three large language models (GPT-5, Llama 3.1 8B, and ModernBERT). Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B achieved the best results and demonstrated particular strength on subskills with highly separable proficiency levels with balanced labels across levels, while lower performance was observed for subskills that required detection of subtle distinctions between proficiency levels or imbalanced labels. Our exploratory work represents an initial step toward scalable assessment of critical thinking skills across authentic educational contexts. Future research should continue to combine automated critical thinking assessment with human validation to more accurately detect and measure dynamic, higher-order thinking skills.

articles.title: Fidelity Before Structure: Verbatim Chunks Beat Lossy Artifact Extraction in Long-Conversation LLM Memory
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.00821v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A growing class of conversational-memory systems compresses dialogue history into structured artifacts (extracted facts, decisions, or events). The premise is that distilled structure retrieves better than raw text. We test this premise with a controlled ablation. Within one fixed retrieval--rerank--reasoning pipeline, we swap only the stored representation (LLM-extracted typed artifacts versus verbatim conversation chunks) and hold the model, retriever, reranker, and judge constant. Verbatim chunks win by 15.9 points on LoCoMo (43.9% vs. 28.0%) and by 22.0 points on LongMemEval-S (67.4% vs. 45.4%). A semantic graph does not recover the gap, and six confound controls reproduce the effect. The mechanism is lossy distillation rather than structure per se. Accuracy tracks how much source text survives in the store, and the extracted-artifact pipeline does not beat naive RAG in overall accuracy (chunks do abstain worse; see Limitations). For the extraction designs we test, structured memory should augment verbatim text rather than replace it. Adding artifacts alongside chunks costs no detected accuracy, while substituting them forfeits the gap. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tao-hpu/cog-canvas.

articles.title: Interpreting and Controlling Model Behavior via Constitutions for Atomic Concept Edits
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.00092v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce a black-box interpretability framework that learns a verifiable constitution: a natural language summary of how changes to a prompt affect a model's specific behavior, such as its alignment, correctness, or adherence to constraints. Our method leverages atomic concept edits (ACEs), which are targeted operations that add, remove, or replace an interpretable concept in the input prompt. By systematically applying ACEs and observing the resulting effects on model behavior across various tasks, our framework learns a causal mapping from edits to predictable outcomes. This learned constitution provides deep, generalizable insights into the model. Empirically, we validate our approach across diverse tasks, including mathematical reasoning and text-to-image alignment, for controlling and understanding model behavior. We found that for text-to-image generation, GPT-Image tends to focus on grammatical adherence, while Imagen 4 prioritizes atmospheric coherence. In mathematical reasoning, distractor variables confuse GPT-5 but leave Gemini 2.5 models and o4-mini largely unaffected. Moreover, our results show that the learned constitutions are highly effective for controlling model behavior, achieving an average of 1.86 times boost in success rate over methods that do not use constitutions. Our open-sourced code can be found at https://github.com/google-deepmind/atomic_concept_edits

articles.title: WAXAL: A Large-Scale Multilingual African Language Speech Corpus
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.02734v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advances in speech technology predominantly favor high-resource languages, leaving speakers of Sub-Saharan African languages underserved. To bridge this divide, we introduce WAXAL, an open, large-scale speech dataset spanning 27 African languages representing over 100 million speakers. WAXAL comprises over 14,100 hours of speech collected in partnership with African academic and community organizations to build local research capacity: an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) corpus with 2,340 hours of transcribed, image-prompted natural speech across 19 languages (plus ~11,760 untranscribed hours) and a studio-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) corpus of ~247 hours across 15 language configurations. We empirically benchmark three architecturally distinct ASR models -- Gemma 3n 2B, Whisper-Large-v3, and MMS-1B-all -- across the 19 ASR languages on strictly speaker-disjoint splits. Fine-tuning on WAXAL yields substantial gains, reducing macro-average WER by up to 58% for Whisper-Large-v3, 56% for Gemma 3n 2B, and 17% for MMS-1B-all (and Character Error Rate by up to 70%). WAXAL-fine-tuned models generalize zero-shot to three out-of-distribution benchmarks: FLEURS, Mozilla Common Voice, and Sunbird SALT. Finally, an LLM-as-judge semantic evaluation confirms that fine-tuning preserves speaker intent beyond surface-level transcription metrics. WAXAL is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/WaxalNLP.

articles.title: TERMINATOR: Learning Optimal Exit Points for Early Stopping in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.12529v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which enables them to generate intermediate thinking tokens before arriving at the final answer. However, LRMs often suffer from significant overthinking, spending excessive compute time even after the answer is generated early on. Prior work has identified the existence of an optimal reasoning length such that truncating reasoning at this point significantly shortens CoT outputs with virtually no change in performance. However, determining optimal CoT lengths for practical datasets is highly non-trivial as they are fully task and model-dependent. In this paper, we precisely address this and design Terminator, an early-exit strategy for LRMs at inference to mitigate overthinking. The central idea underpinning Terminator is that the first arrival of an LRM's final answer is often predictable, and we leverage these first answer positions to create a novel dataset of optimal reasoning lengths to train Terminator. Powered by this approach, Terminator achieves significant reductions in CoT lengths of 14%-55% on average across four challenging practical datasets: MATH-500, AIME 2025, HumanEval, and GPQA, while outperforming current state-of-the-art methods and reducing inference latency by more than 2x compared to the original LRM.Project page: https://terminator-llm.github.io

articles.title: CAF-Score: Calibrating CLAP with LALMs for Reference-free Audio-Text Alignment Evaluation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.19615v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: While Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have advanced audio understanding and generation, robustly evaluating audio-text alignment remains difficult: reference-based metrics require costly annotations, while Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP)-based reference-free metrics frequently overlook syntactic errors and fine-grained details. We propose CAF-Score, a reference-free metric that calibrates CLAP's coarse-grained semantic alignment with the fine-grained comprehension and syntactic awareness of LALMs. Because CAF-Score scores an audio-text pair symmetrically, one configuration applies to both alignment directions: audio captioning evaluation (the BRACE benchmark) and text-to-audio (TTA) generation evaluation (the RELATE and PAM benchmarks), with a single fusion weight selected once on BRACE and transferred without re-tuning. Across all three human-annotated benchmarks, CAF-Score improves agreement with human judgments over standalone CLAP in the large majority of CLAP-LALM combinations (and in all combinations with the strongest LALM backbone), and outperforms standalone LALM metrics on the main captioning benchmark. It also remains competitive with reference-based metrics in challenging scenarios.

articles.title: Automated Code Efficiency Optimization via Agent Skill Mining
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.27850v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Code efficiency is a fundamental aspect of software quality, yet how to use large language models (LLMs) to optimize correct programs remains challenging. Prior approaches rely on one-shot rewriting, retrieved exemplars or instructions, fine-tuning, or candidate search. In this paper, we present EffiSkill, a two-stage framework that models recurring slow-to-fast transformations as Operator Skills: persistent cards that record a transformation's intent, applicability, procedure, expected effect, and risks. Stage I distills frozen, language-specific skill libraries from slow/fast program pairs. Stage II diagnoses a new program, retrieves relevant skills, composes alternative plans, and generates up to eight candidates. These steps finish without candidate-execution feedback; public tests then filter and rank candidates, and held-out private tests determine reported correctness and speedup. Across 623 EffiBench-X tasks per language, two backbones, and separate Python and C++ evaluations, EffiSkill achieves the highest observed OPT@1 and OPT@8 among the compared methods in all four settings. Its OPT@8 margins over the strongest baselines range from 4.98 to 12.52 percentage points. These results support broader successful optimization coverage for the complete skill-guided pipeline under a shared output budget.

articles.title: Supporting Calibrated Reliance in AI-Assisted Decision-Making: Different Strategies for Different Tasks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.03237v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As AI systems increasingly support human decision-making, a central challenge is determining what information helps people recognize when to rely on AI predictions and when to question or override them. Across three controlled human-subject studies spanning abstract visual reasoning with RAVEN matrices and deductive logical reasoning with LSAT problems, we examine how different forms of AI support affect performance in AI-assisted decision-making. A multi-stage reveal study shows that AI predictions and explanations can affect objective accuracy and subjective confidence differently. In visual reasoning, LLM explanations do not improve accuracy beyond the predicted answer alone, and no additional support format significantly outperforms prediction-only support; predicted probabilities show the highest descriptive accuracy and error recovery, while a derived selective-automation policy provides a higher-performing reference benchmark. In language-based logical reasoning, by contrast, LLM explanations yield the highest accuracy and error recovery, outperforming expert-written explanations and probability-based support. These results suggest that the effectiveness of AI support strategies depends on the task setting. Human--AI interfaces should instead be designed to support calibrated reliance and effective error recovery by matching the form of assistance to the task and the evidence available to users.

articles.title: On the Price of Privacy for Language Identification and Generation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.07238v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models train on sensitive user data, so we ask what differential privacy (DP) costs in language learning. We study private language identification and generation in the agnostic statistical setting. For identification, privacy is free: at every fixed $\varepsilon$, pure DP and $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP with $\delta\ge n^{-O(1)}$ keep the non-private rate $\exp(-r(n))$ for every $r(n)=o(n)$. For generation, the price depends on what is public. With a public witness bound, pure DP loses at most a factor $\Theta(\min\{1,\varepsilon\})$ in the exponent, and on suitable two-language collections the optimal rate is $\exp(-\Theta(\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\,n))$. Without such a bound, pure DP can lose the exponential rate itself, already for two languages: every rate $\exp(-o(n))$ stays achievable, but no exponential rate is. On these collections, $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP keeps an exponential rate if and only if $\log(1/\delta)=o(n)$. Three facts about pure DP drive the proofs. It turns a robustness margin into an exponentially small error. It obeys a private form of Le Cam's two-point bound. And it cannot see the absence of a string.

articles.title: Appear2Meaning: A Cross-Cultural Benchmark for Structured Cultural Metadata Inference from Images
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.07338v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Museum records express how people understand heritage objects through cultural and historical relations. Recovering these human attributions from images is a technical challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce Appear2Meaning, a cross-cultural benchmark of 750 museum objects for image-only recovery of title, culture, period, origin, and creator. Its evaluation framework distinguishes field-level from complete-record compatibility and uses human validation for semantic judgement. Across nine VLMs, mean field accuracy is 36.16--49.82%; 7.20--17.02% of records have all four contextual fields compatible, and 2.13--7.87% have all five, including title. For the two tested models, image-only input yields 12.6--32.2 percentage points higher reference compatibility for culture, period, and origin than a museum-and-title-only control.

articles.title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.07789v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents have increasingly focused on repository-level software engineering (SWE) tasks, leading to various agentic workflows, training methods and failure analysis. Interestingly, rather than directly generating or evaluating edit patches, these approaches first examine and improve intermediate information signals collected during agent exploration, including Reproduction Test, Regression Test, Edit Location, Execution Context, and API Usage. Although different studies examine different subsets of these signals, no work has systematically compared their relative effectiveness in improving final task success or measured the remaining space for improvement in each signal. To address this gap, this work quantifies the contributions of both oracle and agent-extracted signals to final task success and measures the gap between current agent-found signals and their oracle counterparts. We hope our findings could suggest future research emphasis in SWE agents. We release our source code and oracle-signal dataset as a reusable methodology to benefit future signal analysis of SWE agents.

articles.title: Seeing but Not Thinking: Routing Distraction in Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.08541v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have achieved remarkable performance on vision-language tasks. However, we identify a puzzling phenomenon termed Seeing but Not Thinking: models accurately perceive image content yet fail in subsequent reasoning, while correctly solving identical problems presented as pure text. Through systematic analysis, we first verify that cross-modal semantic sharing exists in MoE architectures, ruling out semantic alignment failure as the sole explanation. We then reveal that visual experts and domain experts exhibit layer-wise separation, with image inputs inducing significant routing divergence from text inputs in middle layers where domain experts concentrate. Based on these findings, we propose the Routing Distraction hypothesis: when processing visual inputs, the routing mechanism fails to adequately activate task-relevant reasoning experts. To validate this hypothesis, we design a routing-guided intervention method that enhances domain expert activation. Experiments on three multimodal MoE models across six benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements, with gains of up to 3.17% on complex visual reasoning tasks. Our analysis further reveals that domain expert identification locates cognitive functions rather than sample-specific solutions, enabling effective transfer across tasks with different information structures.

articles.title: The Granularity Axis: A Micro-to-Macro Latent Direction for Social Roles in Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.06196v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are prompted to adopt social roles from individuals to institutions, but whether their representations encode this difference in social granularity remains unclear. We discover a contrast-based Granularity Axis, the difference between mean macro- and micro-role hidden states, that aligns with the dominant geometry of role space: in Qwen3-8B, its cosine with PC1 is $0.972$, and PC1 explains $52.6\%$ of the variance. Across 75 roles at five levels, with 90,000 role-conditioned and 1,200 default responses per model, projections increase monotonically and remain stable across layers, prompts, and response-quality filters. The structure transfers to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and scales to Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, whose PC1 shares are $45.99\%$ and $31.23\%$. Independent five-rater validation ($\alpha=0.961$) preserves the ordering; identical continuations and affect/formality controls confirm scale-related variation beyond generated wording. The axis is also behaviorally causal: positive steering moves Llama from $2.00$ to $3.17$ on a five-point macro scale for prompts admitting local responses. Steering strength and stability depend on the model's default operating regime. Together, these findings establish social granularity as a representational primitive: a continuous, ordered, causally manipulable direction organizing role-conditioned generation across model families.

articles.title: Contrastive Identification and Generation in the Limit
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.06211v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In identification in the limit (Gold, 1967), a learner reads positive examples and must eventually name the target hypothesis; in generation in the limit (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024), it must eventually produce new positive examples. We study a weaker, relational signal: each observation is an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$ with $h(x)\neq h(y)$, such as a cannot-link constraint or a dissimilar-pair label, and the learner never learns which point is positive. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. (1) For every corruption budget $k$, known or unknown, we characterize exactly the identifiable classes. Incomparable hypotheses must cover the domain and share more than $2k$ points, and Angluin's tell-tale sets must survive the loss of $2k$ points. Every unbounded budget makes any two hypotheses confusable. (2) A contrastive closure dimension characterizes uniform generation. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.

articles.title: LatentRouter: Can We Choose the Right Multimodal Large Language Model Before Seeing Its Answer?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.11301v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have heterogeneous strengths across OCR, chart understanding, spatial reasoning, visual question answering, cost, and latency. Effective MLLM routing therefore requires more than estimating query difficulty: a router must match the multimodal requirements of the current image-question input with the capabilities of each candidate model. We propose LatentRouter, a router that formulates MLLM routing as counterfactual multimodal utility prediction. Given an image-question query, LatentRouter extracts learned multimodal routing capsules, represents each candidate MLLM with a model capability token, and performs latent communication between these states to estimate how each model would perform if selected. A distributional outcome head predicts model-specific counterfactual quality, while a bounded capsule correction refines close decisions without allowing residual signals to dominate the prediction. The resulting utility-based policy supports performance-oriented and performance-cost routing, and handles changing candidate pools through shared per-model scoring with availability masking. Experiments on MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench show that LatentRouter outperforms fixed-model, feature-level, and learned-router baselines. Additional analyses show that the gains are strongest on multimodal task groups where model choice depends on visual, layout-sensitive, or reasoning-oriented requirements, and that latent communication is the main contributor to the improvement. The code is available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/LatentRouter.

articles.title: HEED: Density-Weighted Residual Alignment for Hybrid Vision-Language Model Distillation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.17093v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Distilling vision-language models into faster hybrid architectures, such as 3:1 Mamba-2/attention mixes, is now standard practice for making inference efficient. Aggregate benchmarks suggest that this works but they hide selective failures. When we distill Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct into a 3:1 Mamba-2/attention hybrid, student model stays within 2 points of the teacher across visual reasoning benchmarks like MMStar, MMBench, and MMMU-Pro, while dropping 13 points on optical-character-recognition and document tasks. The student can still understand the scene but loses the fine-grained text needed to answer. We localize much of the failure to a specific kind of position. In a high-resolution image, most patches are sky, wall, or smooth texture, while a small fraction carries text, edges, object boundaries, or other local details. In a token-level diagnostic, the top 10% highest-density patches have 3.6x larger residual drift than the bottom 10% lowest-density patches and 3.5x larger teacher-masking answer contribution. Uniform weighting devotes many loss terms to low-information background patches, whereas sparse answer bearing patches receive no special protection. The required intervention is minimal: we replace uniform residual alignment with density-weighted residual alignment, using patch self-dissimilarity as a training-free proxy for position importance. We call this HEED. Compared with normal end-to-end distillation, HEED increases performance by 8.7 points on OCRBench v2 and 5.13 points on a 10-benchmark average. The gain is realized on different teacher models. After standard post-training, the student reaches teacher-level performance on the 10-benchmark average. HEED adds no parameters and no inference-time cost. Hence, the student maintains the hybrid architecture's 4.12x throughput and 68% memory saving at 128k context. Code is available at https://github.com/jha-lab/HEED.

articles.title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.17634v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Prompt injection is the most critical vulnerability in deployed AI agents. Despite recent progress, we show that the prevailing defense paradigm (data-instruction separation) both fails to detect attacks that operate through contextual manipulation and degrades contextually appropriate behavior. We then recast prompt injection via the lens of Contextual Integrity (CI), a privacy theory that judges information flow compliance with contextual norms. This explains types of attacks that current defenses attempt to patch and predict advanced ones future agents will face. We develop unique benign and attack scenarios that force an agent to violate the norms by (1) misrepresenting the flow, (2) manipulating norms, or (3) mixing multiple flows. This reframing suggests an impossibility argument: an adversary can always construct a context under which a blocked flow appears legitimate, or a defender who tightens norms will block genuinely legitimate flows. Our findings suggest that current research addresses a shrinking fraction of future attack surfaces. Instead, through CI, we offer a principled framework for evaluating context-sensitive failures, and designing CI-aware alignment for frontier autonomous agents.

articles.title: SAMark: A Self-Anchored Text Watermarking with Paragraph-Level Paraphrase Robustness
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.25796v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Semantic-level watermarking (SWM) improves robustness against text modifications by treating sentences as the basic unit. However, robustness to paragraph-level paraphrasing remains difficult because such attacks globally disrupt watermark signals by changing sentence order. In this work, we propose SAMark, a self-anchored watermarking framework that removes the dependency on sentence order by establishing a step-independent green region in semantic space. To improve detectability, we introduce a multi-channel hyperbolic scoring mechanism that amplifies watermark signals while suppressing noise from weakly aligned candidates. We further propose a diversity-aware filtering strategy that combines hard filtering with soft regularization, extending beyond simple n-gram repetition filters to address semantic redundancy. Experimental results show that SAMark achieves up to 90.2% TP@FP1% under typical paragraph-level paraphrasing attacks, outperforming the strongest prior baseline by more than 30% on average, while maintaining generation quality competitive with unwatermarked text and breaking the robustness-quality trade-off that limits prior methods. Our code will be released at [this URL](https://github.com/Z1zs/SAMark).

articles.title: Do Coding Agents Deceive Us? Detecting and Preventing Cheating via Capped Evaluation with Randomized Tests
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.07379v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A growing failure mode in agent evaluation and training is that models can achieve high evaluation scores (e.g., test pass rates) by exploiting shortcuts instead of solving the intended task, making these scores deceptive. This makes evaluation scores unreliable as measures of true task-solving ability. We propose CapCode, a framework for constructing coding datasets with randomized tests whose best achievable non-cheating score is deliberately capped below 100%. This capped-score design gives evaluation scores a clearer interpretation: scores substantially above the cap are implausible and therefore provide evidence of cheating. To prevent cheating, we propose CapReward, a reward design based on the CapCode principle to discourage optimization beyond the cap. Experiments across multiple datasets show that CapCode detects cheating while preserving performance ranking of models, and CapReward reduces cheating behavior, yielding models that better follow the intended task specification.

articles.title: HandwritingAgent: Language-Driven Handwriting Synthesis in Scalable Vector Space
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.18788v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Teaching machines to emulate natural handwriting styles remains an open challenge, as it requires synthesizing stroke sequences that dynamically vary in shape, texture, pressure and script - not only across individuals, but also within a single person's handwriting. Attempts at this challenge have largely explored deep learning methods in both online and offline settings. However, these approaches are often constrained by style-specific architectural choices, heavy reliance on large datasets, high compute costs, and a lack of flexible control over writing styles through natural language. To this end, we introduce HandwritingAgent, a language-driven agent that can synthesize natural handwriting sequences directly in Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) format with no need for style-specific training. The agent leverages a large reasoning model to geometrically analyse and autoregressively generate target handwritten glyphs as stroke sequences in a discrete grid canvas environment. Generation is conditioned on texts provided in either conversational or non-conversational mode, along with a reference handwriting-style image. Experiments on diverse handwriting tasks spanning imitation, recognition, multi-lingual handwriting synthesis, and generation of complex handwritten maths and science expressions indicate substantial improvement in performance, with HandwritingAgent matching or surpassing state-of-the-art generative handwriting models, while providing a more efficient, controllable, and generalizable synthesis method.

articles.title: RAS: Measuring LLM Safety Through Refusal Alignment
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.25750v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Repeated safety evaluation of open-weight large language models requires generating and judging responses for many related checkpoints. We introduce RAS (Refusal Alignment Score), a representation-based, reference-relative indicator of harmful-request refusal computed by the five-stage SafeVec procedure. SafeVec extracts layer-wise refusal directions from an aligned reference model, measures their alignment in related targets, and calibrates a score from 0 to 100 using behavioral attack success rates (ASR) from reference and calibration models. Subsequent target scoring uses input forward passes alone. Across 18 held-out variants from the Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, RAS correlates with $100(1-\mathrm{ASR})$ (Pearson 0.934, Spearman 0.851) and achieves 83.0% pairwise ordering agreement. Across five prompt configurations for the Llama reference, directions have mean cosine similarity 0.939. With calibration ASR already available, setup-inclusive evaluation of five targets achieves a speedup of 3.2 to 80.5 times over the specified behavioral protocol. These results support refusal alignment as an efficient signal for screening related checkpoints and prioritizing behavioral audits.

articles.title: Cited Web Sources in LLM Answers about Brands: A Multilingual Audit
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.25787v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Displayed citations make part of generative search observable, but they do not reveal its complete retrieval process. This audit covers three archived datasets containing 167,551 URL-bearing citation entries across 128 brands, 13 languages and 12 home markets. In the principal Nordic-Baltic component, 3,863 of 21,033 registrable domains account for 80% of 131,514 citations. Wikipedia leads in 11 of 12 query languages. A recovered, separate brand-associated website classification retains 131,512 entries: 108,410 (82.4%) fall outside its brand-associated category and 23,102 (17.6%) inside. This classification does not establish legal ownership. In the full 57-brand Polish aggregate, four recruitment hosts receive 637 citations against 297 for Polish Wikipedia. The results show why normalization, classification rules and denominators belong in citation audits. They describe displayed links without estimating causal effects on brand reputation.

articles.title: From Weights to Features: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Activation Regularization for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.26629v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Weight-protecting regularizers such as elastic weight consolidation (EWC) are a standard defense against catastrophic forgetting; however, in the sequential fine-tuning of large language models, they exhibit a stability-plasticity tradeoff that penalty tuning cannot resolve. We attribute this limitation in part to polysemanticity: because each weight participates in many unrelated concepts, a per-weight importance score has difficulty isolating the knowledge that requires protection. We instead regularize in activation space, using a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) as a fixed dictionary of approximately monosemantic features. We formulate continual learning as constrained optimization over feature drift, with a stability constraint on the features to be preserved and a plasticity constraint on the features used by the current task, and we show that the resulting squared-hinge loss is a regularized Lagrangian relaxation of this problem, with EWC as a special case. A replay variant measures drift on 200 stored sequences per previous task, whereas a data-free variant stores only a 197 KB feature mask per task, versus 6.5 GB for EWC. On TRACE (Gemma-2 9B, Llama-3.1 8B) and MedCL (Gemma-2 9B), the replay variant matches or exceeds SAE-based feature distillation at approximately one third of its per-step cost, and the data-free variant attains the highest mean overall performance among methods that store no previous-task data and add no task-specific parameters. Task-relevant units are linearly separable in the SAE basis but not in the neuron basis (ROC-AUC of 0.87-0.88 versus 0.50), and weight-space protection constrains the features of other tasks nearly as strongly as those of the protected task.

articles.title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.01523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors---memory capture and memory retention---and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

articles.title: Beyond Satisfaction: Learning Associations Between Content, Reviews, and Well-Being
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.02539v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recommendation algorithms shape what people consume online, yet they are primarily optimized for star ratings, likes, and sentiment, signals of user satisfaction. Whether these signals capture what is good for users, beyond momentary preference, remains largely unexamined. Well-being offers an alternative target grounded in psychology that extends beyond satisfaction. We operationalize it as immediate and enduring expressions of the five PERMA facets in reviews. Empirically, immediate positive emotion and engagement cluster as more hedonic (pleasure-oriented), while relationships, meaning, accomplishment, and enduring positive emotion and engagement behave as more eudaimonic (meaning- and growth-oriented). Analyzing 13.7 million Goodreads reviews and the content of 16 thousand books, we study how PERMA expressions differ from satisfaction targets and which book content features are associated with them. First, satisfaction signals (star ratings and review sentiment) correlate moderately with immediate hedonic well-being (r = .43-.50) but less with its enduring expressions (r <= .28), and have almost no association with eudaimonic facets (r <= .09). Second, book content features are more strongly associated with PERMA facets (r up to .46) than with satisfaction signals (|r| <= .15). Content associated with immediate hedonic well-being differs from that associated with enduring and eudaimonic well-being: third-person pronouns and past-focused language relate positively to immediate engagement (d=1.14 and 1.05) but negatively to every enduring facet (d down to -1.58 and -1.32), while prosocial and achievement-oriented language relate to relationships and accomplishment (d=.45 and .96). These findings suggest that satisfaction signals capture only part of the well-being users express, and that well-being-informed targets could lead platforms to recommend substantially different content.

articles.title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.28591v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Coding agents learn from and are measured on executable tasks, but building such tasks from repository history usually means rebuilding an environment at an old revision for every task, which is costly and brittle. We observe that a merged pull request (PR) can instead be undone on today's code: removing the effect of a bug fix or feature from a maintained revision recreates the same task inside an environment that already builds and runs. We present Change2Task, which converts merged PRs into verified tasks on an up-to-date revision of the same repository. It reconstructs the pre-change state by patch reversal, code mapping, or agent-based rewriting, and keeps a task only if its target tests pass, fail, and pass again across the healthy, task, and restored states. From 1,130 PRs spanning bug fixing, feature addition, test generation, API migration, and security repair, Change2Task builds 900 verified tasks, recovering 29% more than SWE-smith's PR Mirror on matched bug-fix candidates. The reconstructed tasks preserve the evaluation signal: in aggregate, four coding agents solve 41.1% of tasks on both the original and reconstructed versions, with 89.7% per-task agreement. Sharing modern environments across tasks further reduces setup time by 58% and storage by 71%. On 11 private industrial repositories, Change2Task yields 1,000 tasks on which the strongest model reaches only 14.6% Pass@3.

articles.title: A False Average: Pooled CoT-Monitor Accuracy Conceals a Reasoning-Dependent Fragility
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.00583v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are reported by their aggregate accuracy on a pool of reward hacks. We show that this number is a false average. On Terminal Wrench, about 77% of hacks are given away by the actions alone, and the monitor's pooled accuracy is dominated by them; on the remaining 23%, which an action-only monitor misses, the same monitor is fragile. We expose the fragility with a controlled attack: we rewrite only the agent's reasoning to read as good-faith engineering, leaving every command and output byte-identical. One gradient-free rewrite drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on that subset from about 95% to between 4 and 11%, while the pooled rate falls only about 25 points, near what the subset's share of the pool times its collapse predicts. The rewrite stays truthful about what happened and lies only about intent, so the trace-only monitors we test recover little, even when warned about the attack; of our defenses, only information from outside the trace helps much. The attack transfers across monitor and agent families, and the dataset's own hack labels show the same gradient with no monitor in the definition. Live agents told to hack on 27 tasks, with no monitor feedback, produce hollow hacks, but a monitor calibrated on each model's own honest solves catches nearly all of them. Applying the same rewrite to these live hacks keeps all 111 action-visible ones caught and lowers catch on the 16 whose actions score below 0.5 only from 16 to 13: the effect lands where the false average predicts, but the collapse stays a controlled result. A linear probe on a surrogate monitor's activations out-reads its verdict on the obfuscated hacks (AUC up to 0.98), but a behavioral control shows this edge does not, by itself, mean the monitor knows more than it says. Monitor accuracy should be reported on the reasoning-dependent subset, where the defense is load-bearing.

articles.title: LangChoiceBench: Measuring and Explaining Programming-Language Choice in LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.06041v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit strong Python preferences when generating project-level code, but there is currently no systematic way to measure this behaviour across new models. To bridge this gap, we introduce LangChoiceBench, a project-level code-generation benchmark for measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. LangChoiceBench covers 28 projects across seven software areas where Python is often a poor default. We evaluate 25 diverse LLMs and find that Python remains heavily over-selected, recommendation-implementation consistency is low, and smaller open-weight models generally show stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. We further analyse 9,826 reasoning traces and find that most Python choices are automatic or driven primarily by ease, rather than explicit consideration of project requirements. In a smaller but important set of cases, models fabricate contextual support for choosing Python - a failure mode we call phantom evidence - or produce code that contradicts the language selected in their own reasoning.

articles.title: How Diverse Are Layered Safeguards? Estimands and Measurement for Ensembles of LLM Jailbreak Defenses
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.28327v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Practitioners protect large language models (LLMs) by stacking safeguards: a likelihood filter, a guard classifier, hidden-state probes, a decoding-time intervention. Such a stack is an ensemble of learned detectors, and ensemble theory states when combination pays: when members fail on different inputs. Stacking is recommended throughout the LLM security literature, but this condition has not been measured for any pair of safeguards.
  The condition is three quantities, not one, and conflating them is why it has resisted measurement. Separately optimized attacks license only a claim about which \emph{behaviors} are jointly vulnerable; the identity that governs a deployed stack is written over shared \emph{inputs}; and neither predicts what an adversary attacking the assembled pipeline achieves. We define the three estimands, give an estimator for each, and supply two controls: the correlation between two independent runs of the same attack, which sets the level a pair must clear, and a multilevel model separating detector diversity from behavior difficulty.
  On a seven-layer stack and two open-weight targets, no pair of safeguards is distinguishable from the correlation that two independent runs of the attack produce with no safeguard present, and behavior difficulty explains much of what remains. A second attack family, an attacker model rewriting its own prompts, reaches that verdict independently on a thirtieth of the budget and overturns the practical one: the only member that blocked the first adversary admits 0.19 under the second, against 0.03. Diversity between neural safeguards is measurable, but it and any member's strength are properties of a (stack, adversary, target) triple.

articles.title: The Structure of Quantization Damage in LLMs: Why the Next Bit Should Be Spent Globally
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.01587v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is widely used to reduce the cost of serving large language models (LLMs), but its accuracy cost is uneven and is often tuned per model. We study where quantization damage occurs and how to allocate a small additional precision budget. Using causal mixed-precision intervention as ground truth (raise each layer to 8-bit in turn and measure the accuracy it recovers) across 9 open-weight models in 4 architecture families, we test 3 intuitive hypotheses: that quantization damage lives in task circuits, where the model computes, or in weight statistics. None of them predicts which layers benefit from restored precision. Recovery is instead diffuse: for 8 of 9 models, recovering 75% of the gap takes roughly half the layers; the lone exception, Qwen3-8B, is sharply concentrated. At a matched precision budget, spending it globally on finer quantization granularity beats locally repairing the most recoverable layers for all 8 group-128-compatible models (all but OpenLLaMA, whose width rules out group-128), by 21-52 points, including the concentrated Qwen3-8B. We report 2 secondary findings: the residual is budget-limited (8-bit is near-lossless in our evaluation across RTN, GPTQ, and AWQ), and the location of peak recovery correlates with architecture within a family, though not across families. Within this budget setting, global granularity is a better default than selectively protecting critical layers. More broadly, cheap signals that correlate with quantization damage do not necessarily identify where restoring precision improves accuracy; this must be tested with causal intervention.

articles.title: ViSAR: Training-Free Adaptive-$k$ Retrieval for Document Visual Question Answering
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.02486v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Document Visual Question Answering (DocVQA) often leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), where late-interaction encoders are commonly used to identify document pages relevant to a user query, before answer generation by a Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM). Existing approaches typically retrieve a fixed top-$k$ number of pages regardless of query complexity, which increases LVLM latency and may degrade answer accuracy when fewer pages would be enough. We introduce ViSAR (Visual Semantic Activation Retrieval), a training-free, budget-aware adaptive-$k$ retrieval method for late-interaction visual document retrieval. ViSAR operates directly in the embedding space to construct a query-conditioned page-level similarity matrix that highlights query-relevant semantics and dynamically determines the number of pages to retrieve, within a given page budget. We evaluate our method across multiple datasets, encoders, and LVLMs. ViSAR retrieves compact, query-adapted page sets that reduce end-to-end RAG latency by up to 58.9\%, with no statistically significant accuracy loss and significant gains in several settings, compared with fixed top-$k$ and adaptive retrieval heuristics. Furthermore, we show that the similarity matrix structure correlates with answer accuracy, suggesting future directions for retrieval quality-aware document understanding.

articles.title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.11900v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning depends not only on metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape, but also on topological relations that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Cognitive science identifies these relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet foundation-model evaluations largely focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. We introduce MindTopo, a benchmark of topological intuition across five properties grounded in cognitive science and formal topology, namely continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots. MindTopo evaluates each property at two cognitive levels. Reasoning asks a model to identify topological relations or infer how they change. Planning instantiates a foundation model as a closed-loop agent whose policy selects environment actions. MindTopo provides a Core Set of 3,900 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types, split into an Easy and a Hard level, and an Extended Set of 11,035 original instances. On the Core Set, we benchmark 13 multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and study agent configurations augmented with image and video generation, covering seven video generative models in planning settings. Every MLLM performs better on reasoning than on planning. On the Easy level, where human scores are available, the strongest model trails humans in both reasoning and planning. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and reach solved endpoints, yet none of the 1,890 evaluated video rollouts passes all process-validity checks.

articles.title: Large Language Models Develop Belief State Geometry In-Context
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.17376v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on next-token prediction exhibit remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities, yet the representations that support ICL remain poorly understood. We consider such representations in a controlled setting: prompting LLMs with data emitted from hidden Markov models (HMMs) and probing for the corresponding belief state -- the posterior distribution over the HMM's hidden states given the observed token history. Across six open-source LLMs prompted with data from 40 HMMs selected for non-trivial belief structure, we find that belief states are linearly decodable from residual stream activations, with peak probe $R^2$-values of 0.83-0.99 across HMM and LLM combinations, ranging from early to late layers. To establish functional relevance, we intervene directly on the probe-identified subspace via patching and steering, resulting in downstream prediction quality on the order of the untampered model, while controls degrade performance substantially. Together, these results provide representation-level evidence that ICL in open-source LLMs approximates optimal Bayesian prediction over a context-inferred generative model. More broadly, our findings extend prior results linking input-distribution structure to activation geometry: from toy networks trained explicitly on HMM data to production-scale LLMs.

articles.title: Attribution Gaps in Zero-Training LLM+OVOD Pipelines: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the CAAP--SNAP Discrepancy
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.32567v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LAOD and similar zero-training LLM+open-vocabulary-detector (OVOD) pipelines score two things separately: class-agnostic localization accuracy (CAAP) and semantic naming accuracy (SNAP). The two consistently diverge, and nobody has asked why. This paper asks why, on the full 5,000-image COCO-Val split (27,273 detections) rather than the small subset the original work evaluated on. Object visual complexity turns out not to be the driver -- small and occluded objects are, if anything, localized better than large ones. Vocabulary novelty is: once the LLM's wording falls outside the detector's native category set, localization accuracy falls from 80.9% to 31.6%. That drop is not spread evenly across unfamiliar phrasing, though. Almost all of it comes from cases where the novel wording actually names a different object than the one COCO annotated (true synonyms still score 89.3%; semantically unrelated "noise" labels score 12.0%). A closer look at a further failure subset tells a similar story: 78-88% of what looks like complete localization failure is really the model correctly finding a real object that COCO's non-exhaustive 80-category scheme simply never labeled, not hallucination. Swap the detector backbone (YOLO-World for Grounding DINO) or the LLM (Gemma-3 for Qwen2.5-VL) and both the effect and its rough size hold up, so this looks like a general property of the pipeline family rather than a quirk of one model pairing. The upshot is that a large share of the apparent CAAP--SNAP gap traces back to closed-category annotation limits rather than a real grounding failure, which matters for how we detect hallucination, analyze failure modes, and design evaluation for grounded multimodal systems meant to work in the open world.

articles.title: SearchJev: A Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.05107v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Search agents repeatedly make short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions. Using generative language models for these decisions introduces latency and unreliable confidence. We present SearchJev, a calibrated System-1 model that separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. We propose Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD) to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and improve the reliability of decision confidence. In a dual-system search agent, SearchJev handles short decisions and delegates uncertain judgments to System 2, which retains planning, query generation, and answer composition. We also introduce SearchDecision-Bench, a benchmark unifying six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. On SearchDecision-Bench, SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models, achieves 5.2-5.3 times faster decisions, and reduces average expected calibration error by 41-74%. On BrowseComp-Plus, the dual-system agents achieve a 3.7-4.7 times speedup in active search time while improving answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.

articles.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.17727v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

articles.title: Forecasting Brand Mentions in LLM Answers: Frozen Predictions Evaluated from Hours to Weeks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.19608v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Companies and agencies now monitor which brands large language models (LLMs) name when buyers ask for recommendations. Answers vary between runs, so a single check can mislead and repeated checks cost money. We extend an earlier 20-day replication to ask how well past brand mentions predict later ones over seven weeks. We froze probabilistic forecasts before each of four prospective collection waves of Gemini 3.1 Pro answers to the same 54 buyer questions: nine question families in English, Estonian and Finnish, each for two markets, with four of 12 tracked brands per question. The waves were collected between 1.5 hours and 52 days after the history used by the earliest forecast, and each scored 648 brand and answer labels from 162 answers. A smoothed per-question history achieved a Brier score of 0.0599 at 1.5 hours, against 0.1131 for a per-brand rate and 0.25 for a constant 0.5. A pooled rate clipped to 0.05--0.95, named as the challenger before its first test, scored 0.0259 after 8 hours, 0.0269 after 30 days and 0.0328 after 52 days. Of the brand and question cells named in all or none of the earlier answers, 94.5% to 97.5% kept that pattern in each later wave, and none switched from always to never or back. With a search instruction, 100 of 162 answers returned search activity, compared with 1 of 540 earlier Pro answers; mentions stayed predictable (Brier 0.0563), and Pro history predicted a smaller model's answers less well (0.0787). Human coding agreed with 298/300 sampled automatic labels; two coders agreed on 99/100 shared items (kappa = 0.98). The results cover one provider family, a fixed candidate set and lexical mentions. They support per-question history as the baseline that any forecasting or monitoring method for LLM brand mentions should beat.

articles.title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Looped Transformers on Permutation Traversal
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.24135v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows H hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.

articles.title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00606v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Attribution graphs predict sparse autoencoder (SAE) ablations to first order on the active features, but a TopK SAE passes only its k largest preactivations, so small changes often swap active features. On five public TopK SAEs, zeroing one feature changes the active set of the next layer's SAE in 74% to 89% of cases. Our margin graph adds the first order change to every downstream preactivation, then selects the k largest again. On Pythia-70M the margin graph cuts the median error of predicted activations, relative to their exact change, from the attribution graph's 0.739 to 0.121, 84% lower. Exact recomputation of 48 interventions runs 3.5 times faster than the margin graph on our GPU. Patched into Pythia-70M with the clean reconstruction error, the margin graph's activations predict the change in the subject verb agreement logit difference with 1.95 times the attribution graph's mean error, on interventions above a fixed floor. Between seeds of our SAEs, which share one auxiliary loss coefficient, sparse feature maps recover 85% of a graph's squared norm on active features but 47% with each graph masked to its own, 38 percentage points less. Unmasking the inactive tenth nearest the TopK threshold recovers 73% of the masking loss, against 11% for a random tenth, so the margin to that threshold decides how ablations change activations and what graphs carry between seeds.

articles.title: Do Benign-Trained Hidden-State Probes Detect Tool Errors Under Adversarial Conditions?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.11172v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Repeatedly training language models on their own generated data may create a synthetic-data feedback loop in which errors and distributional biases are reintroduced into subsequent training datasets. This paper studies that process in biomedical question answering (QA) using PubMedQA and two Qwen2.5 model sizes, 0.5B and 3B parameters. The study compares a recursive synthetic-data condition, in which generation G(k+1) is trained on answers produced by G(k), against a Human-Control condition that repeatedly uses the original human training data. The study evaluates across four generations from G0-G3 with two random seeds (42 and 123) and a fixed evaluation set of 1,000 expert-labeled samples. The evaluation includes disease and chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, lexical and semantic similarity, answer length, repetition rate, and other evaluation metrics. The Recursive condition for both model sizes and both seeds showed larger declines than the Human-Control condition in disease entity F1, chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, ROUGE-L, and cosine similarity. Under the fixed no-repeat 3-gram decoding constraint, the main observed behavioral change was increased answer length, while the measured 3-gram repetition rate did not increase. The magnitude of the difference-in-change was larger for the 3B model than for the 0.5B model. This difference was particularly apparent in disease F1, context-supported rate, cosine similarity, and answer length. These results show domain-specific changes associated with using recursive synthetic-data training in biomedical QA, but do not establish clinical hallucination rates or universal model collapse.

articles.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.11995v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon

articles.title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.12412v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research typically tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and to our knowledge not with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.

articles.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.15108v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of a claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks normalization and makes algorithmic conversion non-transitive.
  We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($irrel : \Pi P{:}Prop.\,\Pi p,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, $\Pi$-covariant subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, compile to unification-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$), and match declarative typing.
